s: Part four.
Plan mode versus direct execution.
By the end of this part, you'll know when to plan first, when to just do the work, and why plan mode is a habit and not a lock.
Plain version.
If you ask a builder to knock through a wall, you'd like to see the drawing before the sledgehammer comes out.
Not because the builder is careless.
Because the drawing is the cheapest place to find out you meant the other wall.
Now ask the same builder to change a lightbulb, and get a drawing back.
Something has gone wrong with the process.
So the question is never whether planning is good in general.
It's whether a wrong first attempt would cost more than the drawing.
The technical name is plan mode.
In plan mode, Claude researches and proposes, without editing.
It reads files and runs exploratory commands.
Then it writes a plan.
And edits stay blocked until you approve.
How do you enter it?
Three ways.
Press Shift+Tab.
Prefix a single prompt with /plan.
Or start Claude with claude --permission-mode plan.
To make it the default for a project, set permissions.defaultMode to plan in the committed .claude/settings.json.
When the plan arrives, you have three choices.
Approve it into automatic editing.
Approve it into manual approval of each edit.
Or keep planning.
And pressing Ctrl+G opens the plan in your own editor, so you can correct it before Claude acts.
The notes call that the cheapest intervention in the whole workflow.
The deciding test is the one-sentence test.
If you can describe the change in one sentence, and it sits in one file, and the path is obvious, execute directly.
Plan when any of these is true.
The change spans several files.
There are several valid approaches.
You don't know the code.
The area is risky, like authentication or billing.
Or the change is hard to reverse, or architectural.
The supporting pattern is explore, plan, implement, commit.
Four steps.
One.
Explore, with reading prompts only.
Two.
Plan, and edit the plan.
Three.
Approve and implement, while checking against the plan.
Four.
Commit.
Quick recap before the questions.
Plan mode reads, proposes, and waits for you.
The one-sentence test decides whether you need it.
Question one.
Practice question D3-014.
Here's the scenario.
A production error log shows a stack trace.
It points to an off-by-one error in a paginate function, in a single file.
The fix is obvious.
A regression test already reproduces the bug.
And the hotfix must ship within the hour.
Plan, or execute?
Take a second.
The answer.
Execute directly.
Fix the function, run the regression test, and show the passing output.
Plain version.
If a lightbulb has blown, you replace it.
You don't ask an architect for drawings.
Drawings are for knocking through walls, where a mistake is expensive to undo.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: enter plan mode first, because anything going to production deserves a plan.
Why?
The notes call this planning theater.
The round trip costs more than the change, and it delays the hotfix.
Wrong: launch an Explore subagent to map every caller first.
Why?
That's discovery for unclear scope.
And the stack trace has already localized the defect.
Wrong: start with the interview pattern.
Why?
That's for ambiguous requirements.
And the expected behavior is already encoded in the failing test.
The constraint words are clear stack trace, single file, obvious fix, and within the hour.
And notice that the correct answer includes showing the passing test output.
That's evidence rather than assertion.
It's the theme of part five.
Hold on to this line.
If you can say the diff in one sentence, just do it, and show the test passing.
Question two.
Practice question D3-015.
The opposite case.
Here's the scenario.
An engineer who joined last week must move a data extraction pipeline from thirty regex-based parser files to a schema-driven approach.
Regex means pattern-matching code.
There are at least two credible designs.
And a wrong first attempt would touch every parser, and be painful to unwind.
Plan, or execute?
Take a second.
The answer.
Start in plan mode.
Let Claude read the parsers and propose a phased plan.
Edit it with Ctrl+G.
Then approve and implement.
Every trigger is present.
Unfamiliar code.
Competing designs.
Thirty files.
And an expensive failure.
Plain version.
Before rewiring a whole house, you ask the electrician for a drawing.
You mark up the parts you disagree with.
And only then do you let them start.
Going room by room with no plan, and saying we can always rip it out, is how you pay twice.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: execute directly across all thirty files with acceptEdits, the mode that accepts edits automatically, relying on git to revert.
Why?
Unwinding thirty files of rework is exactly the cost planning avoids.
And you get an unreviewable diff.
Wrong: start in plan mode, but keep bypass permissions on to avoid prompts.
Why?
This misunderstands what plan mode is.
We'll see why in a moment.
Wrong: fan out one non-interactive run per parser immediately, because each file is independent.
Why?
Fanning out before the design is chosen, and proven on a sample, reproduces an unvetted approach across every file.
We'll meet that sequencing rule again in part five.
Hold on to this line.
Uncertain approach, many files, unfamiliar code, costly failure.
Plan first, and edit the plan.
Now the concept the exam uses to separate practitioners from people who read the brochure.
Question three.
Practice question D3-016.
This one is pick two.
Here's the scenario.
A team lead wants every contributor's sessions to start in plan mode by default.
The lead is also counting on plan mode to guarantee that nothing under a migrations folder is ever edited without approval.
Including in sessions where some engineers enable bypass permissions.
Which two actions?
Take a second.
The answers.
First.
Set permissions.defaultMode to plan in the committed project settings file.
That makes it the team default, and shares it through version control.
Second.
Protect the migrations folder with a permission deny rule, or a PreToolUse hook, instead of relying on plan mode.
Here's why.
Plain version.
Asking every builder to show you a drawing before starting is a good habit.
But it doesn't lock the cupboard with the fuse box.
If nobody may ever touch the fuse box, you put a lock on it.
The drawing habit covers everything else.
In exam terms.
In sessions where bypass permissions are available, plan mode's blocks are not enforced.
So an edit Claude attempts while planning will run.
Hold on to this line.
Plan mode is a workflow control, not a security boundary.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: rely on plan mode for the guarantee, because it blocks edits in every mode.
Why?
False, for the reason you just heard.
Wrong: add always start in plan mode to the lead's personal CLAUDE.md.
Why?
User scope is never shared.
And prose cannot set anyone's permission mode.
Wrong: plan mode stops Claude reading files, so write the plan from a description.
Why?
False.
Plan mode lets Claude read and explore.
What it blocks is edits, until approval.
A related trap from the notes' exam items.
An option says: execute a large refactor directly with acceptEdits, the mode that accepts edits automatically, because plan mode blocks the edits the task requires.
Why is that wrong?
It misdescribes the mechanism.
Approving a plan exits plan mode into an editing mode.
Plan mode does not prevent the eventual edits.
Now a contrast.
This is where two ideas are most often confused.
Plan mode, versus a permission rule or hook.
Plan mode changes what you approve, and when.
A permission rule or hook changes what the tools are physically able to do.
When a stem says default, habit, or workflow, think plan mode.
When it says guarantee, never, or must not, think deny rule or hook.
The same split appears in part one: advice versus enforcement.
And it will appear again in part five.
That's part four.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Plan mode is a habit, not a lock.
Anything that must not happen needs a permission rule or a hook.
Coming up in part five: iterative refinement for progressive improvement.
